description: We are a highly motivated team, from UADY university, studying Software Engineering, Computer Science, and Chemical Engineering. We are very enthusiastic about participating in this hackathon and we are ready to build something great. Our diverse academic backgrounds allow us to solve problems from multiple perspectives, and we are eager to learn and ready to work hard!
summary: Lunar Mission is a desktop web app that helps mission planners, educators, and the public decide where and when to land near the Moon’s south pole. Users pick one of 13 curated sites (Artemis III candidate regions plus Apollo 11, Apollo 17, Chang’e 3, and Chandrayaan-3), click the globe, or type coordinates, then set a mission window between 2025 and 2035. The app shows the Sun and Earth against the real local horizon and condenses solar power, direct-to-Earth communication, and terrain slope into one Suitability Index with a traffic-light verdict and explained vetoes. It targets the challenge’s key scenario: when a launch slips, planners can shift the window or compare sites in seconds instead of juggling several expert tools. This matters because at the south pole the Sun and Earth skim only a few degrees above the horizon, so a small change in place or date can decide whether a mission has power and contact.
details:
Lunar Mission turns any of 13 landing sites and a chosen mission window into a 360° view of the local lunar horizon, with the Sun and Earth drawn at their true angular size. It shows how much of each disc clears the terrain and gives the next sunset and Earthset. It reports sunlight, Earth visibility, longest darkness, and slope, scores them with agreed weights, and explains every veto (Earth visible under 25%, sunlight under 5%, darkness over 48 h, mean slope over 10°, far side). A 2D view shows the proposed landing zone and its error margin over official LROC images, and a timeline shows daily light and contact bands.

How it works: an offline Python pipeline uses NASA NAIF SPICE kernels (DE421, MOON_ME, no refraction) to compute hourly Sun and Earth positions from 2025 to 2035. South-pole sites use LOLA topography (PGDA 78 and 90) for horizons that account for lunar curvature up to 150 km, plus slope; historical sites use a smooth-sphere horizon. Positions match JPL Horizons within 0.0001°. A FastAPI backend serves the data and computes the index.

What we hope for: to make what-if landing planning fast and explainable, and to show why the south pole is so demanding.

Tools: Python, SpiceyPy, NumPy, Rasterio, SciPy, FastAPI, TypeScript, React, Three.js (React Three Fiber), Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Vite, and Claude Code.
